To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) path analyses and structural equation models, as used in most social science, are invalid, because they make unjustifiable assumptions about the nature of causal relationships; and (2) the use of investigations to make causal conclusions is invalid because it is impossible to separate the effects of selection bias and other forms of confounding from those of causal variables

(a) The use of data from correlational investigations (e.g., path analyses) to make causal inferences is logically indefensible and statistically unjustified; (b) Such methods can only be used to suggest hypotheses that then must be tested by proper experimentation; and, (c) The methods of structural equation modeling (e.g., LISREL) do not overcome these problems, and are logically and mathematically equivalent to the methods of path analyses

(i) the use of path analysis or other methods of causal inference in correlational data to make causal inferences is not logically defensible; (ii) the use of correlational methods in the Coleman studies to make policy recommendations is not defensible statistically; (iii) correlational methods can only suggest hypotheses which then must be tested by proper experimental designs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the logical and statistical flaws of the methods of Page, Keith and associates, and their application to the Coleman studies.
the use of data to draw conclusions.
the logical and statistical problems of the use of investigations to make causal conclusions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the methods of path and structural analysis cannot be used to make causal conclusions.

(a) Investigations can never establish causality, but can be used to suggest possible hypotheses for testing by experiments, (b) Experiments can be used to establish causality and to refute false causality hypotheses, and (c) Investigations and experiments are complementary and should be used together.
the methods of structural equation modeling and path analysis are not logically or statistically defensible. They should not be used to make causal inferences from correlational data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the methods of path analyses and structural equation modeling are logically flawed and should never be used to make causal conclusions.
